# How the ranking works

*The rules behind every number on the site. If you would rather have the tour than the rules, read [Start here](#f=05_start_here) first.*

**Not investment advice.** This is an independent research project that maps the AI supply chain from public sources. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security, and figures can be wrong or out of date.

This page explains every number the site derives, so that you can argue with the method rather than the output. The knowledge base is hand-curated: each node carries stats, and each stat carries a value, unit, date, source, a confidence grade and a method. Nothing on the page is a bare number.

## Grades and methods

- **Grade A**: a filing or an official dataset (10-Q, 20-F, USGS, FRED, Eurostat, Epoch CC-BY data). **B**: a company statement, guidance, or a reputable dataset (investor-relations releases, LBNL, IEA). **C**: trade press or analyst estimates (TrendForce news, SemiAnalysis public pieces, Sacra). **D**: our own estimate, triangulated from other figures; always shown with a range.
- **Method**: *measured* (reported), *guided* (company guidance), *estimated* (analyst or our estimate), *derived* (computed from other stats), *fetched* (pulled automatically, for example market caps from Yahoo).
- **Freshness**: every stat has an as-of date. Market caps older than 45 days, other financials older than 150 days and capacity figures older than 400 days are flagged stale (an amber dot on the map, "stale" in the side panel).

## What earns a node a place

This test is applied on every build, and it bites: nodes that were in earlier builds and are not here now (Gefion, Ørsted, Vestas, several Nordic data-centre operators) failed it. A node is in the graph only if it takes part directly in its layer's transformation and meets at least one of: at least 10% of a layer's global supply or a top-5 position by a credible source; sole-source or one of at most three suppliers of a component; a counterparty in a disclosed AI contract of at least $1bn or 100 MW; a top-20 token consumer by disclosed or estimated spend, or the clearest example of a cell in the Demand 2×2; or a market segment that carries a series the dashboards use. Being Danish or Nordic is not a reason on its own: Energinet's grid pause and the Danish adoption statistics qualify because the dashboards read them; a bank or a brewer that merely uses Copilot does not. Nodes that fail the test are kept on file marked retired, and the build drops them and their links, so a decision can be reversed.

## Layer stats

- **Fill** is how full a layer's capacity is: a curated summary with its own source (for example ASML's two-year waitlist, TSMC N3 above 100%), or the mean of node utilisation where nodes report it. **Supply gap** is the shortfall as a share of demand where a source states one (CoWoS 10%, InP 70%, 800G optics 40-60%).
- **Capacity growth** and **demand growth** are per-year rates with sources. **Growth gap** is capacity growth *minus* demand growth, so a **negative gap means demand is outrunning capacity** and is the case to worry about; the dashboards colour negative amber and positive green, and the layer card writes it out as "lagging" or "ahead". **Pipeline to 2028** sums planned additions through two years ahead as a share of tracked capacity.
- **Concentration** is a Herfindahl index (HHI, 0-10,000) computed per product market inside the layer (etch, deposition, EUV resist, HBM), never across the whole layer, using disclosed shares or capacity. The layer shows its tightest market.
- **Valuation aggregates** use listed companies only: median and market-cap-weighted forward P/E (share price divided by expected earnings over the next twelve months), median trailing P/E, median revenue growth, gross margin and drawdown, and the sum of market caps. Yahoo forward P/E is excluded for Korean listings because its figures there are unreliable.

## The bottleneck score (0-5)

Each node gets up to seven sub-scores between 0 and 1. Missing inputs are skipped; the score is the weighted mean of what is present, times five. A score is only shown when the inputs present carry at least 35% of the weight, and the side panel shows this **confidence** next to the score.

| Input | What it measures | How it is scored | Weight |
|---|---|---|---:|
| U utilisation | how full the node is | node utilisation, else the layer's fill: ≥95% → 1.0, ≥85% → 0.7, ≥75% → 0.4, else 0.1 | 0.22 |
| L lead time | how long a new order waits | (weeks − 12) / (104 − 12), capped at 1 | 0.13 |
| B backlog cover | backlog relative to annual revenue | backlog ÷ revenue, capped at 3 years, ÷ 3; or book-to-bill − 1 | 0.10 |
| C concentration | how few suppliers exist | half the product market's HHI (÷10,000) plus half the node's own share | 0.18 |
| A substitutability | whether an alternative exists | 1 minus the maturity of the best alternative (none 0, lab 0.2, pilot 0.4, ramping 0.7, mature 1) | 0.15 |
| R relief distance | years until planned capacity meets demand | (relief year − this year) ÷ 4, capped at 1 | 0.10 |
| S upstream rationing | how full the tightest supplier feeding the node is | the supplier's utilisation or its layer's fill, same buckets as U; falls back to the layer below | 0.12 |

A curated **override** and a written rationale can sit beside the computed score; both are shown. The **layer score** is the share-weighted mean of its nodes' effective scores.

Why S exists: [accelerators](#l=accelerators) still score 2.5 while every layer feeding them scores 3.5 to 4.9, because NVIDIA has mature alternatives (A = 0) and reports no utilisation. S makes a node inherit the tightness of its suppliers, so "can buyers get the chips" shows up in the score. It narrows the anomaly; it does not remove it.

Known limits: the score is ordinal, not a probability; it rewards disclosure (a private company with no numbers scores nothing); and it does not know prices, which is why the Bottlenecks page pairs it with forward P/E.

## Flows

Ribbons sum the links between two groups. For the money measure, links point the way cash moves: a buyer pays its supplier, a tenant pays its landlord, a financier pays the recipient. Opposite flows between two groups are netted and marked ⇄; any remaining cycle is broken by dropping its smallest link, and the page says how many. Values are contract totals as disclosed, not annual run-rates, unless the link says otherwise.

## Demand 2×2

**Horizon** is short when the unit task is below roughly three to four hours of expert time (the METR 80% time horizon), long above. **Bounded** work stops adding value once done correctly, so demand converges on the cheapest adequate model; **unbounded** work keeps adding revenue or capability with more tokens, so the frontier is required. Each consumer carries a **share of spending funded by the AI boom itself**: the share of its token spend that is paid for by the AI boom (coding 0.6, AI R&D 1.0, trading 1.0, enterprise agents 0.25, consumer 0.05, bounded back office 0). All of these are our estimates (grade D) until labs disclose their customer mix.

## Refresh

The same rules, grades and scores run on every chain the site covers. Market caps and P/E ratios (Yahoo) and 33 FRED series are pulled automatically; each build validates the knowledge base, derives everything above and republishes the page data. The validator flags stale stats, isolated nodes and share sums above 100% inside a bundled market, and those warnings are fixed or noted before a build goes out.

# Start here

*A five-minute tour for your first visit. Read [How the ranking works](#f=00_method) afterwards if you want to argue with the numbers rather than the conclusions.*

## What this site is

One picture of the AI buildout, from the mines to the companies that buy tokens. The September build these reports were written from held **345 companies, products and markets in 18 layers**, joined by **381 links** (today: 348 and 400) that are supply, lease, finance or token flows. The bottom layer is minerals and gases; the top layer is the businesses paying for frontier tokens; capital runs beside the whole thing as a side rail.

Every number on the site carries a date, a source and a confidence grade: **A** a filing or official dataset, **B** a company statement or reputable dataset, **C** trade press or analyst, **D** our own estimate. Nothing is a bare number. Across the build there are 1,578 graded figures: 15% A, 23% B, 54% C, 7% D. That mix is the honest summary of how much of this is hard.

The question the whole thing is built to answer: **where does the buildout physically run out, who owns that point, and what is it priced at?**

## The tour, tab by tab

1. **[Overview](#v=overview)**: the landing page. The headline findings on one screen, with a way into each of the views below.
2. **[Map](#v=map)**: the whole chain, one band per layer, minerals at the bottom and token buyers at the top. Click any circle or layer card for the detail panel and its sources.
3. **[Bottlenecks](#v=bottlenecks)**: the layers ranked by the gap between demand growth and capacity growth, paired with what each one costs.
4. **[Demand 2×2](#v=demand)**: the 85 token consumers sorted by whether their work keeps paying for a better model.
5. **[Countries](#v=country)**: where the chain is headquartered, where it physically produces, and a simple AI scorecard per country.
6. **[Flows](#v=flows)**: $347.8bn of disclosed commitments and the contracted power, drawn as ribbons.
7. **[Cost of capital](#v=rates)**: the 10-year Treasury yield against our estimated fair range, credit spreads, and a table of warning signals.
8. **Findings**: these written reports, one per view.

## The three numbers

**4.9 out of 5: [lithography subsystems](#l=litho_subsystems).** The tightest layer in the graph. Every EUV machine ASML sells depends on optics from [Carl Zeiss SMT](#n=zeiss_smt) (score 4.8) and drive lasers from [TRUMPF](#n=trumpf) (score 5.0). Zeiss High-NA output has not accelerated since 2024. The layer holds six nodes and only one of them is listed: [Lasertec](#n=lasertec), at 35.8x forward earnings. Zeiss SMT, TRUMPF, Cymer, VDL ETG and Gigaphoton are private or subsidiaries, so the tightest point in the chain has no listed pure play.

**−120 points: the [accelerator](#l=accelerators) growth gap.** Accelerator demand is growing +117% a year while unit capacity is growing −3%. The growth gap is capacity minus demand, so a negative number means demand is outrunning capacity: at −120 points this is the widest such gap anywhere in the graph. It does not mean chips are scarce in units: it means the dollars are going up far faster than the volume, because each generation carries more silicon and memory. The physical scarcity sits in the layers underneath: [wafer fabrication](#l=wafer_fab) scores 4.5, [advanced packaging](#l=packaging_substrates) 3.6, [engineered materials](#l=engineered_materials) 3.5.

**~24%: AI's share of US investment-grade bond issuance in the first half of 2026**, against 8.5% in 2025 and 3.8% in 2024. Hyperscaler long-term debt is around $518bn, up from roughly $270bn at the end of 2024, and debt now funds 32% of hyperscaler capex against 9% in FY2024. The buildout has stopped being an equity story. See [Cost of capital](#v=rates).

## How to read a layer card

The left column of the [map](#v=map) carries one card per layer. From the top of the card down:

- **`L7 · 15 nodes · score 2.5`**: the layer's position from the bottom, how many nodes it holds, and its bottleneck score out of 5. The score is the share-weighted mean of its nodes' scores; a blank means the layer lacks the capacity data the formula needs, not that it is loose. Seven of the 18 layers are blank.
- **The fill bar**: how full the layer's capacity is, and the supply gap where a source states one. `100% · gap 10%` means running flat out and still 10% short of demand.
- **`cap +8%/yr  dem +41%/yr ▼ lagging`**: capacity growth against demand growth, with the verdict. Amber "lagging" is the thing to look for: it is the layer falling behind this year, not in theory.
- **Tracked capacity** in the layer's own unit, then the **median forward P/E** (share price over the next twelve months' expected earnings) **and the sum of market caps** of the listed companies in it. Tightness and price read together: a tight layer priced cheaply and a tight layer priced richly tell different stories.
- **Risks and estimates only**: how many curated risks the layer carries, and how many of its nodes have no measured figure at all, only estimates.

Click the card for the layer panel, which adds the evidence grade mix, the concentration index for the tightest product market inside the layer, the top-scoring nodes and the sources behind each stat. Click a circle for a company: size is market cap (or market share for products), colour is the segment, a dashed outline means estimates only, an amber dot means a stale figure.

## Where the bottlenecks are

Seventy-five of the 345 nodes carry a bottleneck score. The tightest, in order:

| Node | Score | Layer | Why |
|---|---:|---|---|
| [TRUMPF](#n=trumpf) | 5.0 | Litho subsystems | Sole source of EUV drive lasers |
| [Global 300 mm fab capacity](#n=fab_300mm_capacity) | 5.0 | Wafer fab | The aggregate leading-edge constraint |
| [Carl Zeiss SMT](#n=zeiss_smt) | 4.8 | Litho subsystems | EUV optics; output flat since 2024 |
| [Lasertec](#n=lasertec) | 4.8 | Litho subsystems | EUV mask inspection, effectively alone |
| [Ajinomoto](#n=ajinomoto) | 4.5 | Engineered materials | Over 95% of ABF build-up film |
| [HBM market](#n=hbm_market) | 4.4 | Memory | Three suppliers; 3-4x the wafers per bit |
| [Siemens Energy](#n=siemens_energy) | 4.4 | DC equipment | Turbines and grid equipment, sold out |
| [Large power transformers](#n=transformer_market) | 4.1 | DC equipment | 128-week lead times, prices +77% on 2019 |

Two patterns stand out. First, **the constraint has moved downstream**: the litho and wafer layers are tight and have been for two years, but the layers falling furthest behind their demand now are power and data-centre electrical equipment, at −51 and −33 points: demand grows +60% and +41% a year against capacity at +9% and +8%. Second, **one layer is loosening**: packaging capacity is growing +68% against +49% demand, which is the only place in the graph where capex is currently winning.

## What to click first

1. **[Litho subsystems](#l=litho_subsystems)**, then [Zeiss SMT](#n=zeiss_smt): the single-source constraint that gates every leading-edge fab expansion.
2. **[Flows](#v=flows)**: look at the [accelerators](#l=accelerators) → [frontier labs](#l=frontier_labs) ribbon: $105bn of it is a single commitment from [NVIDIA](#n=nvidia) to [OpenAI](#n=openai).
3. **[Demand 2×2](#v=demand)**: 41 names sit in the top-left cell, where better models keep paying off; 24 sit in the bottom-right, where the cheapest adequate model wins.
4. **[Countries](#v=country)**: the production chart separates countries that build the chain from countries that buy from it.

## What it does not know

- **Seven of 18 layers have no bottleneck score**: networking and optics, servers and cooling, data centres, frontier labs, inference, token consumers and capital. The formula needs capacity or fill data they do not publish.
- **Private layers have no valuation**: frontier labs, inference providers and capital providers carry no market cap or P/E at all.
- **The flow data is thin**: 22 capex links and 17 power links. There is no wafer-allocation flow, no token flow and no equipment-delivery flow.
- **Token spend is almost never disclosed**, so every share of spending funded by the AI boom on the Demand page is our estimate.
- **Credit is index-level**: FRED option-adjusted spreads by rating bucket, plus monthly CDS snapshots. No issuer-level bond prices.

# The chain at a glance

*What the map holds, which layers are tight, and how good the evidence behind each one is. Build of 19 September 2026.*

## Shape of the graph

The graph holds **345 nodes across 18 layers**, joined by **381 edges** and two Sankey flow dimensions (capex and power). Node density varies sharply, and so does the quality of what is behind each layer: the last column is the share of that layer's evidence that is a filing, an official dataset, a company statement or a reputable dataset rather than trade press or our own estimates.

| Layer | Nodes | Score | A+B evidence | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| [Token consumers](#l=token_consumers) | 87 | – | 18% | Much the biggest layer, and much the softest |
| [Data centres](#l=data_centers) | 26 | – | 44% | Landlords, hyperscale, crypto-conversions, Nordics |
| [DC equipment](#l=dc_equipment_construction) | 25 | **4.3** | 38% | Transformers, switchgear, cables, EPC |
| [Engineered materials](#l=engineered_materials) | 22 | 3.5 | 44% | Wafers, ABF, glass cloth, resists, mask blanks |
| [Servers & cooling](#l=servers_cooling) | 20 | – | 41% | No score despite Munters supply constraints |
| [Minerals & gases](#l=minerals_gases) | 18 | 3.4 | 54% | Helium, gallium, germanium, rare earths, InP |
| [Compute providers](#l=compute_providers) | 18 | **4.0** | 42% | Hyperscalers, neoclouds, in-house silicon |
| [Power grid](#l=power_grid) | 18 | 3.1 | 33% | Turbines, renewables, utilities, queue data |
| [Semicap](#l=semicap) | 16 | 3.5 | **61%** | Best-evidenced layer in the graph |
| [Frontier labs](#l=frontier_labs) | 16 | – | 15% | Worst-evidenced layer; no market caps at all |
| [Accelerators](#l=accelerators) | 15 | 2.5 | 33% | Lowest score of any scored layer |
| [Networking & optics](#l=networking_optics) | 15 | – | 38% | No score despite a 50% supply gap |
| [Capital](#l=capital) | 12 | – | 31% | Credit markets and financing segments |
| [Inference & distribution](#l=inference_distribution) | 11 | – | 26% | Routers, API resellers, edge |
| [Packaging & substrates](#l=packaging_substrates) | 11 | 3.6 | 57% | CoWoS, ABF substrates, T-glass |
| [Litho subsystems](#l=litho_subsystems) | 6 | **4.9** | 56% | Tightest layer; five of six nodes private |
| [Memory](#l=memory) | 6 | 3.6 | 38% | Six nodes for a $3.6tn market-cap layer |
| [Wafer fab](#l=wafer_fab) | 3 | **4.5** | 37% | TSMC, Intel Foundry and the global capacity line |

## Tightest layers by score

1. **[Lithography subsystems](#l=litho_subsystems): score 4.9.** Zeiss High-NA optics cadence flat since 2024; fill 100% [TECHREADER_EUV_2026, grade C]. Every EUV system ASML can build is spoken for. Capacity growth of +30% is ASML's own plan; Zeiss output is the limit [C32, grade B]. [TRUMPF](#n=trumpf) scores 5.0, [Zeiss SMT](#n=zeiss_smt) and [Lasertec](#n=lasertec) 4.8.
2. **[Wafer fabrication](#l=wafer_fab): score 4.5.** TSMC N3 utilization above 100%; N2 booked to 2028 [RESEARCH_SA_HW_2026_09_05, grade C]. Demand growth +40% against capacity growth +22%. Three nodes, one of which, [global 300 mm fab capacity](#n=fab_300mm_capacity), scores 5.0.
3. **[DC equipment](#l=dc_equipment_construction): score 4.3.** Orders +41% against capacity +8% [C30, grade A / MGRID_SIEMENS_2026_08, grade C]. [Siemens Energy](#n=siemens_energy) 4.4, [Eaton](#n=eaton) 4.3, [large power transformers](#n=transformer_market) 4.1 on 128-week lead times.
4. **[Compute providers](#l=compute_providers): score 4.0.** Demand +150% against capacity +77% [THESIS_2026_09_12, grade D]. The demand figure is our own estimate, with a 100–250% range: treat the score as directional.

## Evidence quality

Across **1,578 graded figures**: **15% grade A** (filings and official datasets), **23% B**, **54% C**, **7% D**. Just under two in five figures come from a filing or a company.

The softest layers, by share of C and D evidence: [frontier labs](#l=frontier_labs) 85%, [token consumers](#l=token_consumers) 82%, [inference and distribution](#l=inference_distribution) 74%, [capital](#l=capital) 69%, [accelerators](#l=accelerators) 67%, [power grid](#l=power_grid) 67%. The hardest: [semicap](#l=semicap) 61% A+B, [packaging and substrates](#l=packaging_substrates) 57%, [litho subsystems](#l=litho_subsystems) 56%, [minerals and gases](#l=minerals_gases) 54%.

The pattern is consistent and worth stating plainly: **the closer a layer is to a machine, the better the evidence; the closer it is to a model or to money, the worse.** Everything the graph says about frontier labs, inference, capital and token consumers rests on trade press and our own estimates.

## Where to click first

1. **[Litho subsystems](#l=litho_subsystems)**: the single-source optics constraint that gates every leading-edge fab expansion. Click [Zeiss SMT](#n=zeiss_smt) and [TRUMPF](#n=trumpf). Only [Lasertec](#n=lasertec) is listed.
2. **[Wafer fab](#l=wafer_fab)**: the TSMC single point of failure. Click [TSMC](#n=tsmc) for N3/N2 utilization and capex.
3. **[DC equipment](#l=dc_equipment_construction)**: transformer lead times of 128 weeks, with half of 2026 US data-centre openings delayed. Click [Eaton](#n=eaton) for the order data.
4. **[Accelerators](#l=accelerators)**: score 2.5 is the puzzle: demand +117% and unit volume −3%. Click [NVIDIA](#n=nvidia) for the mismatch, and read the [bottleneck report](#f=20_bottlenecks) for why the score is low.

## What is missing

- **No market-cap or P/E data** for frontier labs, inference providers or capital providers: all private, or not equities at all.
- **No bottleneck score for 7 of 18 layers** (networking and optics, servers and cooling, data centres, frontier labs, inference, token consumers, capital), because the formula needs fill or supply-gap data they do not publish. Only 75 of the 345 nodes carry a score.
- **Memory has six nodes** for a layer worth $3.6tn: SK hynix, Samsung Electronics, Micron, Sandisk, CXMT and the HBM market. There is no separate DRAM market node and no Kioxia or YMTC.
- **Flow data is thin**: two dimensions, 22 capex edges and 17 power edges. No wafer-allocation flow, no token flow, no equipment-delivery flow. The GPU-unit dimension that earlier builds carried has gone with the nodes that held it.
- **No live CDS or bond-level prices**; credit spreads are FRED index proxies by rating bucket.
20_bottlenecks:
# Where capacity lags demand

*The growth gap layer by layer, what each tight layer costs, and the risks behind the numbers. Build of 19 September 2026.*

## Growth-gap ranking

For every layer with both capacity and demand growth, the **growth gap** (capacity growth minus demand growth, the same sign the layer cards use) says where the buildout is falling behind this year. **A negative gap means demand is outrunning capacity**; the layer card writes it as "lagging". A positive gap means the constraint is loosening.

| Layer | Demand growth | Capacity growth | Gap (pp) | Fill / supply gap | Score |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|
| [Accelerators](#l=accelerators) | +117% [C10, A] | −3% [PRESENC_GPU_2026, C] | **−120** | – | 2.5 |
| [Compute providers](#l=compute_providers) | +150% [THESIS_2026_09_12, D] | +77% [THESIS_INPUTS_2026_09_11, B] | **−73** | Fill 95% [SAIDX, D] | 4.0 |
| [Power grid](#l=power_grid) | +60% [THESIS_INPUTS_2026_09_11, B] | +9% [RESEARCH_PB_2026_09_05, B] | **−51** | Gap 41% [SECONDWATT_TURBINES_2026, C] | 3.1 |
| [DC equipment](#l=dc_equipment_construction) | +41% [C30, A] | +8% [MGRID_SIEMENS_2026_08, C] | **−33** | Fill 100% [RESEARCH_SA_HW_2026_09_05, C] | 4.3 |
| [Wafer fab](#l=wafer_fab) | +40% [RESEARCH_PLATFORM_2026_09_05, B] | +22% [TF_2026_09_COWOS, C] | **−18** | Fill 100% | 4.5 |
| [Data centres](#l=data_centers) | +77% | +60% | **−17** | – | – |
| [Engineered materials](#l=engineered_materials) | +15% [THELEC_WAFERS_2026, C] | +7% [BIGGO_WAFERS_2026_06, C] | **−8** | Fill 95% [BIGGO_WAFERS_2026_06, D] | 3.5 |
| [Semicap](#l=semicap) | +18% [SEMI_2026_04_300MM_EQUIP, B] | +30% [C32, B] | **+12** | Fill 100% [RIJNBERK_ASML_Q2_2026, C] | 3.5 |
| [Packaging & substrates](#l=packaging_substrates) | +49% [SILICONANALYSTS_FOUNDRY_2026, C] | +68% [TF_2026_09_COWOS, C] | **+19** | Gap 10% [TF_2026_06_COWOS, C] | 3.6 |
| [Frontier labs](#l=frontier_labs) | +150% | +170% | **+20** | – | – |

Three layers carry a demand figure with no capacity figure to set against it: [inference and distribution](#l=inference_distribution) at +300%, [networking and optics](#l=networking_optics) at +58% with a stated 50% supply gap, and [servers and cooling](#l=servers_cooling) at +31%. Their absence from the table is missing data, not a loose constraint.

## Key observations

### The accelerator paradox

[Accelerators](#l=accelerators) post the largest growth gap (−120 pp, demand outrunning capacity by 120 points) and the **lowest score of any scored layer** (2.5). The explanation: NVIDIA data-centre revenue grew +117% [C10, grade A] while unit shipments fell slightly (−3%), because the Blackwell-to-Rubin transition lifts dollars and FLOPs per unit rather than volume. The score formula reads the unit decline as slack. Meanwhile every layer that physically constrains accelerator output scores well above it: [wafer fab](#l=wafer_fab) 4.5, [packaging](#l=packaging_substrates) 3.6, [memory](#l=memory) 3.6, [engineered materials](#l=engineered_materials) 3.5, [litho subsystems](#l=litho_subsystems) 4.9. The layer is demand-unconstrained and supply-rationed by everything around it.

### Two layers loosening

- **[Packaging and substrates](#l=packaging_substrates)**: CoWoS capacity growth (+68%) now exceeds demand growth (+49%), and the gap narrows to about 10% by end-2026 [TF_2026_06_COWOS, grade C]. This is the **one layer where capex is winning**. But ABF substrate utilization is above 95% with orders secured into 2029–30 [TROY_ABF_2026_08, grade C], and T-glass cloth is short 10–20%, so the constraint migrates from CoWoS to the substrate materials underneath it.
- **[Semicap](#l=semicap)**: ASML's capacity growth (+30%) exceeds equipment spending growth (+18%). Utilization is still 100% and the backlog is above EUR 40bn, but tool delivery is catching up with new orders. Loosening on a flow basis, tight on a level basis.

### Tightness against price

| Layer | Fill / gap | Median fwd P/E | Listed market cap | Listed names |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| [Memory](#l=memory) | 95% fill, 8% gap | **6.5x** | $3,575bn | 4 |
| [Servers & cooling](#l=servers_cooling) | demand +31% | 16.3x | $1,433bn | 16 |
| [Power grid](#l=power_grid) | 41% gap | 19.3x | $844bn | 10 |
| [DC equipment](#l=dc_equipment_construction) | 100% fill | 23.5x | $1,464bn | 19 |
| [Litho subsystems](#l=litho_subsystems) | 100% fill | 35.8x | $22bn | **1** |

**Memory at 6.5x forward is the cheapest tight layer by a wide margin**, and the reason is in the layer's own risk list: margins near 86% are cyclical peaks, and memory prices have historically fallen more than 60% when supply arrives [RESEARCH_SA_HW_2026_09_05, grade C]. The multiple is discounting the cycle, not the chokepoint.

**Litho subsystems is the opposite case.** It is the tightest layer in the graph at 4.9, but the 35.8x is a single company: [Lasertec](#n=lasertec), at $22bn. [Zeiss SMT](#n=zeiss_smt), [TRUMPF](#n=trumpf), Cymer, VDL ETG and Gigaphoton are private or subsidiaries. **The tightest point in the chain has no listed pure play.** The nearest listed companies sit one layer away in [semicap](#l=semicap), at 28.1x across $2.1tn.

**Power grid at 19.3x** pairs a 41% supply gap and demand growing +60% against capacity at +9% with a multiple below the DC-equipment layer next to it.

## Top risks by severity

1. **Transformer lead times 128 weeks, generator step-ups 144 weeks, prices +77% against 2019** [DEVTO_TRANSFORMER_2026, grade C], and about half of planned 2026 US data-centre openings delayed or cancelled on transformer and switchgear shortages [RESEARCH_SA_HW_2026_09_05, grade C].
2. **Heavy-duty turbine lead times of three to seven years, a three-firm oligopoly, prices +195% since 2019** [SECONDWATT_TURBINES_2026, grade C]. ERCOT's queue is 474 GW, about 90% data centres, on a roughly 2% request-to-operating funnel; Texas paused new data-centre connections on 3 August 2026 [LATITUDE_ERCOT_2026, grade C].
3. **Leading-edge AI logic is effectively single-sourced from TSMC in Taiwan** [C23, grade B], and CoWoS is the sole packaging path for NVIDIA, AMD and Broadcom accelerators, with NVIDIA taking about 60% of capacity [SILICONANALYSTS_FOUNDRY_2026, grade C].
4. **EML laser and InP wafer shortages set the 1.6T optics schedule**, and NVIDIA's $4bn lock-up of Lumentum and Coherent pushes other buyers past 2027 [TECHTIMES_OPTICS_2026_05, grade C]. The layer's stated supply gap is 50% of demand.
5. **China produces 98% of primary refined gallium and 69% of mined rare earths, and is the leading germanium refiner, all under export controls** [USGS_MCS_2026, grade A; no sourced germanium share]. This is the only grade-A entry in this list.
6. **About 43% of frontier-lab revenue is reflexive** on our own decomposition, within a range of 30 to 64% [THESIS_2026_09_12, grade D]: a 10-point demand shock amplifies to 18 points in a bust.

## Data quality warning

The two layers with the largest growth gaps rely on the weakest evidence. Compute-provider demand growth of +150% is grade D, our own estimate, with a 100–250% range. The accelerator unit decline is grade C. [Accelerators](#l=accelerators) and [power grid](#l=power_grid) both run at 67% C-and-D evidence, and [frontier labs](#l=frontier_labs) at 85%. Any figure marked C or D in the table above could be materially wrong; the A-grade entries are the accelerator and DC-equipment demand figures and the USGS mineral shares, and nothing else.

# Where the money and the megawatts go

*The two Sankey dimensions: disclosed dollar commitments and contracted power. Build of 19 September 2026.*

## Capex flows: $393.1bn tracked

The graph tracks **$393.1bn of disclosed commitments across 22 edges**. Rolled up to layers, where links inside a single layer drop out, that is **$347.8bn across 11 ribbons**. These are contract totals as disclosed, not annual run-rates.

### Largest layer-to-layer ribbons

| From | To | Amount | Share |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| [Accelerators](#l=accelerators) | [Frontier labs](#l=frontier_labs) | $105.0bn | 30% |
| [Compute providers](#l=compute_providers) | [Token consumers](#l=token_consumers) | $53.0bn | 15% |
| [Compute providers](#l=compute_providers) | [Data centres](#l=data_centers) | $46.8bn | 13% |
| [Frontier labs](#l=frontier_labs) | [Compute providers](#l=compute_providers) | $39.1bn | 11% |
| [Capital](#l=capital) | [Compute providers](#l=compute_providers) | $35.1bn | 10% |

| [Capital](#l=capital) | [Data centres](#l=data_centers) | $10.3bn | 3% |

### Concentration of payers and receivers

- **[NVIDIA](#n=nvidia) is the single largest source**: $105bn committed to [OpenAI](#n=openai) plus $20bn to [Groq](#n=groq). That is **$125bn, or 32% of everything tracked, from one company**, and 100% of the accelerators-to-labs ribbon is that one OpenAI commitment.
- **Data centres are the largest net receiver**: $46.8bn from compute providers, $19bn from frontier labs, $14bn from accelerators and $10.3bn from capital, for about **$90bn of inflow**.
- **[CoreWeave](#n=coreweave) is the largest single capital absorber**: $35.1bn from the [DC credit market](#n=dc_credit_market) plus $7bn from [Jane Street](#n=jane_street), $42.1bn in all. It then pays $36.2bn out again to [Applied Digital](#n=applied_digital) and $0.9bn to [Core Scientific](#n=core_scientific). It is a conduit, not a terminus.

### Top entity-level commitments

| From | To | Amount |
|---|---|---:|
| [NVIDIA](#n=nvidia) | [OpenAI](#n=openai) | $105.0bn |
| [xAI / SpaceX Colossus](#n=xai_spacex_colossus) | [Cursor](#n=cursor) | $60.0bn |
| [CoreWeave](#n=coreweave) | [Applied Digital](#n=applied_digital) | $36.2bn |
| [DC credit market](#n=dc_credit_market) | [CoreWeave](#n=coreweave) | $35.1bn |
| [Global DC capacity](#n=dc_market_global) | [Hut 8](#n=hut8) | $26.6bn |
| [OpenAI](#n=openai) | [Microsoft Azure](#n=microsoft_azure) | $24.1bn |
| [NVIDIA](#n=nvidia) | [Groq](#n=groq) | $20.0bn |
| [Anthropic](#n=anthropic) | [TeraWulf](#n=terawulf) | $19.0bn |
| [Anthropic](#n=anthropic) | [xAI / SpaceX Colossus](#n=xai_spacex_colossus) | $15.0bn |
| [AMD](#n=amd) | [Core Scientific](#n=core_scientific) | $14.0bn |

### Circular and netted relationships

The striking pattern is the **labs-clouds-labs loop**. Frontier labs pay compute providers $39.1bn; accelerator makers pay frontier labs $105bn while those labs' entire product depends on buying those same accelerators. [OpenAI](#n=openai) receives $105bn from NVIDIA and pays $24.1bn to [Microsoft Azure](#n=microsoft_azure). [Anthropic](#n=anthropic) pays $19bn to [TeraWulf](#n=terawulf) and $15bn to [xAI / SpaceX Colossus](#n=xai_spacex_colossus) for capacity while receiving compute from AWS and Google, which is tracked in power rather than dollars.

Links point the way cash moves: a buyer pays its supplier, a tenant pays its landlord, a financier pays the recipient. Opposite flows between two groups are netted and marked ⇄, and any remaining cycle is broken by dropping its smallest link.

**[Anthropic](#n=anthropic) alone contracts 12.4 GW**: 5 GW from AWS, 5 GW from Google Cloud, 1 GW of Google TPU, 1 GW of AWS Trainium and 0.4 GW from TeraWulf. That is more than any single hyperscaler's disclosed capacity here, and close to twice Denmark's 7 GW peak grid load.

## What the flow data cannot yet show

- **The GPU-unit dimension has gone.** Earlier builds carried a third Sankey of accelerator units; the nodes that held it did not survive the inclusion test, so the chain now has two dimensions.
- **Wafer allocation**: TSMC's split of N3 and N2 capacity between NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom and Apple is not tracked as a flow.
- **Token flows**: OpenRouter throughput (29.2T tokens a week) exists as a series, not as a source-to-destination ribbon.
- **Equipment delivery**: transformers, switchgear and turbines are tracked as lead times, not as flows from maker to project.
- **Gross, not net**: NVIDIA's $105bn to OpenAI and OpenAI's $24.1bn to Azure are separate ribbons. The net new capital committed to physical infrastructure is smaller than the gross total suggests.
- **Financing is barely covered**: $35.1bn of DC credit and $10.3bn of backstop capital, against $334bn of data-centre bond and loan issuance in 2026 to date. The rest is not disaggregated to borrower level.

# Where the chain sits

*Node counts by headquarters, production exposure, and the single-country dependencies that matter. Build of 24 September 2026.*

## Headquarters concentration

Of the 346 nodes, **203 (59%) are headquartered in the United States**. But headquarters and production are different questions, and the second column is the one that matters: **production exposure** adds up the shares of physical production a country hosts across the chain's tracked markets, so 1.0 is the equivalent of one whole market. It can only see companies that carry a production map, 43 of the 152 producing companies in this chain so far, most of them in the bottom layers; **n/c** marks a country whose zero comes from its own unmapped producers, a gap in our coverage rather than a finding.

| Country | Nodes | Production exposure | Key layers |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| **United States** | 203 | 7.90 | All 18 layers; 67 token consumers, 19 data centres, 15 power |
| **Japan** | 20 | **13.23** | Engineered materials 11, semicap 5, litho subsystems 2 |
| Global (no HQ) | 18 | 1.63 | Market and segment nodes: minerals 6, DC equipment 3 |
| **China** | 17 | 5.22 | Frontier labs 5, minerals 4, networking 3, compute 3 |
| **Taiwan** | 16 | 5.31 | Packaging 7, servers 5, accelerators 2, wafer fab 1 |
| **Germany** | 11 | 4.58 | Engineered materials 4, litho subsystems 2, token consumers 3 |
| **Korea** | 8 | 3.88 | Memory 3, DC equipment 2, semicap 1, packaging 1 |
| **Denmark** | 10 | **n/c** | Token consumers 4, servers and cooling 2, power 1, data centres 1, equipment 1, capital 1 |
| United Kingdom | 6 | 0.20 | Token consumers 3, accelerators 1, data centres 1 |
| Netherlands | 5 | 1.60 | Semicap 3, litho subsystems 1, compute 1 |
| Sweden | 4 | n/c | Servers and cooling 2, token consumers 2 |
| France | 4 | n/c | DC equipment 2, token consumers 1, frontier labs 1 |

**Japan has the highest production exposure in the graph at 13.23 on twenty nodes.** The United States has 203 nodes and 7.90. That gap is the whole argument of this page.

## Critical single-country dependencies

### Japan: the materials position

Japan headquarters **11 of the 22 engineered-materials nodes** and 2 of the 6 litho-subsystem nodes. The sole sources: [Ajinomoto](#n=ajinomoto), over 95% of ABF build-up film from two plants, with prices raised about 30% [BIGGO_AJINOMOTO_2026, grade C]; [Nittobo](#n=nittobo), effectively sole-sourced T-glass cloth, 10–20% short in 2026 widening to 20% in 2027 [TOMS_ABF_2026, grade C]; and EUV resist from JSR, TOK and Shin-Etsu. [Lasertec](#n=lasertec), the only listed litho-subsystem name in the graph, is also Japanese.

### Taiwan: the wafer and packaging chokepoint

[TSMC](#n=tsmc) fabricates essentially all leading-edge AI logic: N3 utilization above 100%, N2 booked to 2028 [RESEARCH_SA_HW_2026_09_05, grade C]. Taiwan also holds **7 of the 11 packaging and substrate nodes** and 5 of the 20 server and cooling ODMs. Production exposure of 5.31 understates the dependency, because TSMC's share of leading-edge by value is closer to 90%.

### Netherlands and Germany: the EUV corridor

[ASML](#n=asml) in the Netherlands, [Zeiss SMT](#n=zeiss_smt) and [TRUMPF](#n=trumpf) in Germany are the EUV triad. The litho-subsystem layer scores 4.9, the tightest in the graph. Zeiss High-NA output has not accelerated since 2024 [TECHREADER_EUV_2026, grade C]. Between them the two countries hold 16 nodes and 6.18 of production exposure, more than China's 5.22 on 17 nodes.

### Korea: the memory pillar

[SK hynix](#n=sk_hynix), [Samsung Electronics](#n=samsung_electronics) and [Micron](#n=micron) (US-headquartered, with fabs in Asia) control the overwhelming majority of HBM. HBM consumes 3–4x the wafer capacity per bit of commodity DRAM and is supply-constrained through end-2027 [C12, grade B], while [CXMT](#n=cxmt) ramps toward about 12% share by 2028 [SACHINA, grade C].

### China: minerals and models, not manufacturing

China produces **98% of primary refined gallium and 69% of mined rare earths** and is the leading germanium refiner, all under export controls [USGS_MCS_2026, grade A; the 77% germanium share used earlier has no source and is withdrawn]. It holds 5 of the 16 frontier-lab nodes and 3 compute providers, and Chinese open-weight models are about 46% of OpenRouter volume [TOKENMAXXING_OR_2026_09, grade C]. It has no leading-edge wafer fab or lithography node in the graph at all. The exposure is upstream and political, not manufacturing depth.

## Denmark and the Nordics

### Denmark: 10 nodes, production exposure not yet measured

Denmark is an **adoption winner and a compute have-not**, and the ten nodes say so. Its production-exposure cell reads **n/c**, not covered: its three producing companies, [NKT](#n=nkt), [Danfoss](#n=danfoss) and [Grundfos](#n=grundfos), carry no production map yet, so a zero would describe our coverage, not Denmark. Denmark does make things for the chain: NKT adds medium-voltage cable at Asnaes [NKT_AR_2025, grade A] and Danfoss makes VLT drives at Graasten [DANFOSS_VLT_ORIGIN_2023, grade B], though most of the production both companies own sits abroad.

- **Enterprise AI adoption 42.0%**, the highest in the EU against a 20% average, up 14.5 points in a year [EUROSTAT_ISOC_EB_AI, grade A]. The [Denmark enterprise AI adoption](#n=denmark_enterprise_adoption) node carries the series.
- **[Energinet](#n=energinet)** held requests for **33.5 GW of new consumption on the transmission grid alone** at the start of 2026, about 60 GW with the distribution networks, against a national peak load of 6.96 GW in 2025 [ENERGINET_AR_2025, grade A]. Data centres, Power-to-X and batteries are about 80% of the growth, and data-centre requests exceed 14 GW against an industry projection of about 1.2 GW installed by 2030 [DCI_DK_14GW_2026, grade C]. No new large-load agreements are signed before the autumn of 2026, and on 4 September 2026 the regulator ordered Energinet to stop applying its maturity and prioritisation criteria until a method is approved [FORSYNINGSTILSYNET_2026_09_04, grade A]. This is the binding fact for anything compute-related in Denmark.
- **[NKT](#n=nkt)** ($7.6bn), power cable, is the only *listed* Danish name in the physical chain, and it sits in DC equipment rather than chain inputs. Its Transmission backlog was EUR 13.0bn at 30 June 2026 (EUR 11.6bn at standard metal prices), not counting over EUR 2.5bn of TenneT framework awards [NKT_H1_2026, grade B].
- **[Danfoss](#n=danfoss)** and **[Grundfos](#n=grundfos)**, both foundation-owned, sit beside Munters and Alfa Laval in servers and cooling. Danfoss sells compressors, heat exchangers, valves and drives into data-centre cooling; its data-centre sales were about 7% of EUR 9.43bn in 2025 and almost doubled [DANFOSS_FY2025_RESULTS, grade B]. Grundfos names data centres a key growth driver of EUR 4.7bn of 2025 revenue [GRUNDFOS_FY2025, grade B].
- **[Novo Nordisk](#n=novo_nordisk)** ($191bn, 12.9x forward), **[Genmab](#n=genmab)** ($21bn) and **[Corti](#n=corti)** are the token consumers, plus the adoption series.
- **[Danish mortgage rates](#n=dk_mortgage_rates)** sits in the capital layer: the 72% variable-rate share is where an AI-driven rise in rates reaches Danish households.

Denmark's scorecard: government debt 27.5% of GDP, adoption score 8.0, compute access 2.0 of 5, composite 6.9, rank 5.

### Nordic neighbours

Five nodes in all. **[Munters](#n=munters)** (Sweden, $2.4bn), CDU supply-constrained with orders up 137% [THESIS_2026_09_12, grade B], and **[Alfa Laval](#n=alfa_laval)** (Sweden, $22.9bn), heat exchangers for liquid cooling, are the two that sit in the physical chain. **[Lovable](#n=lovable)** and **[Klarna](#n=klarna)** (Sweden) and **[1X Technologies](#n=oneex)** (Norway) are token consumers. Sweden reads n/c for the same reason as Denmark, since neither Munters nor Alfa Laval carries a production map; Norway's exposure is 0.10.

Earlier builds carried Nordic data-centre operators, Ørsted, Vestas, Asetek, Nokia and the Gefion national AI centre. They did not survive the inclusion test in this build: a node has to take part directly in its layer's transformation, and cheap power or a national flag is not enough on its own. Danfoss and Grundfos were added on 22 September 2026 because they pass it. **The honest read is that the Nordic physical position in this chain is five companies, all in cooling, drives and cable: Munters and Alfa Laval in Sweden; Danfoss, Grundfos and NKT in Denmark.**

## Export-control exposures

1. **Chinese gallium and germanium**: 98% of primary gallium and the leading share of refined germanium, licensed [USGS_MCS_2026, grade A]. A revocation disrupts compound semiconductors and optics.
2. **ASML export controls**: EUV and advanced DUV restricted to China; the China share shapes ASML's order book [C32, grade B].
3. **Taiwan concentration**: leading-edge AI logic is effectively single-sourced from one island, and overseas-fab margin dilution is a disclosed risk [C23, grade B].
4. **Chinese optics**: most of the top transceiver module makers are Chinese, while the EML lasers and InP wafers that gate 1.6T come from a different, equally narrow set [TECHTIMES_OPTICS_2026_05, grade C].
5. **Helium**: Qatar exports were disrupted in 2026, taking roughly a third of world supply offline with no quick substitute [FOOL_HELIUM_LINDE_2026_04, grade C]. It is the export exposure nobody models.

## The July 2026 episode

From 18 June to 29 July, an equal-weight basket of fifteen AI infrastructure stocks fell 44% on our own calculation while the S&P 500 fell 2.3% over the same dates [THESIS_2026_09_12, grade D]. Two European DC bond deals were pulled; ~80% of data-centre securities issued since early 2025 trade wider than issue [NEOCLOUD_2026_07_30, grade C]. CoreWeave 5-year CDS spiked from 452bp (June) to **855bp** (July), implying ~50% default probability [THESIS_INPUTS_2026_09_11, grade C]. The trigger was the cost of capital, not demand: lab revenue kept compounding through the sell-off.

# Demand 2×2: who keeps paying for the frontier

*The 85 token consumers, sorted by whether more tokens keep buying more value. View: [Demand 2×2](#v=demand). Layer: [Token consumers](#l=token_consumers). Build of 19 September 2026.*

## 1. Shape of the 2×2

The [Demand 2×2](#v=demand) places **85 token-consuming companies**. Throughout, the **AI-boom-funded share** is the share of a company's token spending that is funded by the AI boom itself (for example, an AI start-up spending its investors' money, or a trading desk spending AI-driven profits). The layer itself holds 87 nodes; two are reference series rather than buyers.

| Quadrant | Count | Share | What it is |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Unbounded / long horizon | 41 | 48% | Frontier spenders: frontier tokens are non-negotiable |
| Bounded / short horizon | 24 | 28% | Cheapest model wins: cost-saving, converges on the cheapest model |
| Unbounded / short horizon | 16 | 19% | Volume without lock-in |
| Bounded / long horizon | 4 | 5% | Rare in practice |

**Geography.** United States 66 (78%), then the UK, Denmark and Germany at three each, Sweden, Israel and India at two. **Ownership:** 43 listed, 35 private, 7 subsidiaries. **Nordic names:** [Novo Nordisk](#n=novo_nordisk) and [1X Technologies](#n=oneex) (unbounded/long), [Lovable](#n=lovable) (unbounded/short), [Genmab](#n=genmab), [Corti](#n=corti) and [Klarna](#n=klarna) (bounded/short).

The shape to notice: **the frontier-spender cell is more than twice the cheapest-model cell by count, but the cheapest-model cell is where the listed money is.** The unbounded/long cell is 18 listed names against 23 private; the bounded/short cell is almost entirely listed incumbents.

## 2. Unbounded / long horizon: the spenders

Forty-one names, and three groups carry the cell.

- **Trading and quant (7).** The only category where the share of spending funded by the AI boom is 1.00 across the board. [Jane Street](#n=jane_street) has committed about $7bn to [CoreWeave](#n=coreweave) GPU capacity. [Man Group](#n=man_group) has the lowest forward P/E of any unbounded-task name, at 9.6x. [Citadel](#n=citadel), [Two Sigma](#n=two_sigma) and [Bridgewater](#n=bridgewater) sit beside them; [Goldman Sachs](#n=goldman_sachs) and [JPMorgan](#n=jpmorgan) come in at 0.50 and medium frontier dependence.
- **Coding (6).** [Cursor](#n=cursor), valued at $60bn with about $2bn of ARR, [Cognition](#n=cognition), [Windsurf](#n=windsurf), [GitHub Copilot](#n=github_copilot), [Factory AI](#n=factory_ai) and [GitLab](#n=gitlab). AI-boom-funded share 0.60 throughout [THESIS_2026_09_12, grade D]; frontier dependence high for all but GitLab.
- **Drug discovery and science (7).** [Isomorphic Labs](#n=isomorphic_labs), [Xaira](#n=xaira), [Chai Discovery](#n=chai_discovery), [Recursion](#n=recursion), [Eli Lilly](#n=eli_lilly), [Schrödinger](#n=schrodinger) and [Novo Nordisk](#n=novo_nordisk) ($191bn, 12.9x forward). AI-boom-funded share 0.10: the payoff is gated by wet-lab time, not by token budgets, which is exactly why this is the most durable part of the cell.

The rest: [robot foundation models](#n=physical_intelligence) and [Skild AI](#n=skild_ai) at an AI-boom-funded share of 1.00, a pure loop; [AI R&D](#n=poolside) and [Magic AI](#n=magic_ai), likewise 1.00; chip design ([Synopsys](#n=synopsys), [Cadence](#n=cadence), [Arm](#n=arm_user)); data platforms ([Databricks](#n=databricks) at $190bn and $7bn ARR, [Snowflake](#n=snowflake) at 110.9x forward, [MongoDB](#n=mongodb)); defence ([Anduril](#n=anduril), [Shield AI](#n=shield_ai), [Helsing](#n=helsing)); and autonomy ([Tesla](#n=tesla), [Waymo](#n=waymo), [Figure AI](#n=figure_ai), [1X](#n=oneex)).

**The concentration to watch:** eleven of the 41 names carry an AI-boom-funded share of 1.00, meaning every token they buy is funded by the AI boom itself. Trading and AI R&D are the whole of that group.

## 3. Unbounded / short horizon: volume without lock-in

Sixteen names. Demand is unbounded but value per token is capped, and the buyer can switch model inside a session.

- **Prosumer coding (5).** [Lovable](#n=lovable), [Replit](#n=replit), [Bolt.new](#n=bolt_stackblitz), [Vercel](#n=vercel), [Wix](#n=wix). AI-boom-funded share 0.60, frontier dependence medium: a cheaper model usually suffices.
- **Generative media (4).** [Midjourney](#n=midjourney), about $500m of annual recurring revenue (ARR) with roughly forty employees and no outside funding: the highest-margin AI consumer product in the graph by an order of magnitude. [ElevenLabs](#n=elevenlabs) ($11bn, $500m ARR), [Runway](#n=runway_ai), [Suno](#n=suno).
- **Consumer and commerce.** [Perplexity AI](#n=perplexity) ($23bn, $450m ARR), [Character.ai](#n=character_ai), [Meta AI](#n=meta_ai_product), [Shopify](#n=shopify) (51.9x forward), [Robinhood](#n=robinhood) (35.3x), [Figma](#n=figma) (65.0x), [Datadog](#n=datadog) (77.6x).

This is the most expensive cell in the graph and the one with the weakest moat: median forward P/E above 50x on work the buyer can move to a cheaper model at any point.

## 4. Bounded / short horizon: cheapest model wins

Twenty-four names. "Cheapest adequate model wins", and the mechanism is measurable: effective token prices fell **41% since March 2026** as buyers routed volume away from the most expensive models [RAMP_2026_08, grade B].

| Name | From 1y high | Fwd P/E | Signal |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| [Chegg](#n=chegg) | – | – | Market cap down to $83m; students moved to chatbots |
| [Upwork](#n=upwork) | −87% | 6.2x | Buyers −21.9%, revenue −15.5% y/y [UPWORK_Q2_2026, B] |
| [AppLovin](#n=applovin) | −56% | 14.8x | Ad-auction value per token has a hard ceiling |
| [Intuit](#n=intuit) | −54% | 11.0x | The textbook bounded task |
| [Fiverr](#n=fiverr) | −40% | 6.6x | Same mechanism as Upwork |
| [Adobe](#n=adobe) | −31% | 9.0x | Creative work commoditised at the bottom |
| [ServiceNow](#n=servicenow) | −31% | 27.3x | Still the most expensive name in the cell |

**BPO and IT services** are the purest expression: [Teleperformance](#n=teleperformance) at **4.9x forward**, [Concentrix](#n=concentrix) at **2.3x**, [Infosys](#n=infosys) at 12.8x after cutting guidance to 1.5–3% growth, [TCS](#n=tcs) at 12.9x, [Accenture](#n=accenture) at 12.4x. All at an AI-boom-funded share of 0.00 and low frontier dependence: none of their spend depends on the frontier, and none of their revenue is protected from it.

**Agent-shaped software** is the other half: [Salesforce](#n=salesforce) (Agentforce at $1.2bn ARR, priced at about $2 a resolution), [Workday](#n=workday), [Zendesk](#n=zendesk), [Intercom](#n=intercom), [Sierra](#n=sierra), [Decagon](#n=decagon), [Glean](#n=glean). [Klarna](#n=klarna) ($5.2bn) is the proof point: AI handles two-thirds of enquiries and replaced about 700 full-time roles.

## 5. Bounded / long horizon: the small cell

Four names: [SAP](#n=sap) ($242bn, 21.6x), [Oracle Applications](#n=oracle_apps) ($442bn, 13.3x), [Intuit](#n=intuit) and [Harvey](#n=harvey) ($11bn). The cell is thin because bounded work with a long feedback loop is rare: an ERP migration or a tax year qualifies, and little else does. **Will it grow?** Unlikely in count. Watch SAP and Oracle AI-revenue disclosures for spend growth inside it.

## 6. Placements flagged for debate

Three names carry a "?" on the page. Hover any name to read the reasoning; these three are the closest calls.

1. **[Palantir](#n=palantir)** (unbounded/long). $423bn at 75.7x forward. Model-agnostic, and the moat is data integration rather than the frontier. **Kept** there, because operational agents are genuinely unbounded, but an AI-boom-funded share of 0.25 and medium frontier dependence flag the partial insulation. The valuation is the open question, not the placement.
2. **[Harvey](#n=harvey)** (bounded/long). The per-matter ceiling is bounded; the engagement is long. **Kept.** It moves to unbounded/long if agents start running open-ended legal strategy rather than diligence.
3. **[AppLovin](#n=applovin)** (unbounded/short → bounded/short). Reclassified on 18 September 2026: AXON benefits from better models, but ad-auction value per token has a hard ceiling. Down 56% from its high. **This reclassification is the most debatable placement on the page.**

## 7. Denmark: adoption leader, thin token demand

Denmark leads the EU at **42.0% of enterprises using AI** against a 20.0% average, up 14.5 points in a year [EUROSTAT_ISOC_EB_AI, grade A]. IMF AI Preparedness puts it 2nd of 174.

And it has **three names in the 2×2**: [Novo Nordisk](#n=novo_nordisk) in unbounded/long, [Genmab](#n=genmab) and [Corti](#n=corti) in bounded/short. That is the Danish paradox in its sharpest form: the fastest adoption in Europe, and almost no domestic demand for frontier tokens. [Corti](#n=corti) handles 250,000 patient interactions a day and beats big-lab models on medical coding, but the task is bounded. Genmab's evidence is ChatGPT Enterprise productivity, not discovery.

**The contradiction stands:** no large Danish company has disclosed frontier-model spend or AI-driven revenue. Adoption is grade A; monetisation evidence is grade D. The reading is that Denmark's adoption lead buys *productivity*, not token demand, and the exposure that actually matters is on the other side of the balance sheet: 72% variable-rate mortgages make Danish households among the first to pay for AI-driven rate rises. See [Cost of capital](#v=rates).

## 8. What the data cannot show

- **Token spend is almost never disclosed.** [Salesforce](#n=salesforce) ($1.2bn Agentforce ARR) and [Datadog](#n=datadog) (19 of its 20 largest AI customers above $1m a year) are the only real proxies. Everything else is estimated.
- **Every AI-boom-funded share is grade D, our estimate.** They are unverifiable until a lab discloses its customer mix. The [Anthropic](#n=anthropic) S-1 would be the first hard look.
- **Drawdown data is patchy**: seven per-name figures against roughly $2tn of software value erased between January and April 2026 [THESIS_2026_09_12, grade C].
- **Private marks are last-round, not live**: Cursor $60bn, Databricks $190bn, Perplexity $23bn, Harvey $11bn.
- **The layer is 82% C-and-D evidence**, the second softest in the graph. Read the counts as a map of where this project has looked, not a census of the market.

**Watch:** the Ramp AI Index monthly; Census BTOS biweekly; startup ARR disclosures; and the Anthropic S-1 for the first split of frontier revenue between bounded and unbounded work.
